The waterfalls around Ubud sit in a band to the east and south of the town, mostly within an hour's drive. Tegenungan is the closest and the busiest, with a broad fall and a pool at the bottom. Tibumana and Kanto Lampo, both in Bangli, are smaller and better for getting in the water: Tibumana drops in a single curtain into a clear pool, and at Kanto Lampo the water fans across a stepped rock face that people climb onto for photographs. All of them involve steps down and back up, and the rocks are slippery, so proper sandals or shoes that can get wet are the right footwear. The wet season, November to March, brings the fullest flow but also brown water for a day or two after heavy rain.

Balinese food is built on base genep, the island's spice paste, and eaten from warungs and night markets more than restaurants. Babi guling, spit-roast pig with crackling and spiced rice, is the dish the island is known for; nasi campur is rice with a spoonful of several things; sate lilit is minced meat on lemongrass; and lawar is the chopped salad that comes with most of it. Gianyar's night market opens at about 5:00 in the evening and is the best one near Ubud. Food tours stop at six to ten places for small portions, so arrive hungry, and tell the guide about chilli tolerance early, because Balinese sambal is not mild.

The Tegallalang terraces are twenty minutes north of Ubud on the road to Kintamani, and they are working paddies fed by the subak irrigation system that UNESCO listed in 2012. Before about 8:30 in the morning the valley belongs to the farmers, the paddies are still wet from the night, and it is cool enough to walk down through the terraces and up the far side. By ten the coaches from the south arrive and the road above the terraces becomes a line of cafes, swings and photo platforms. There is a small entry fee at the viewpoint, and farmers along the paths through the fields ask for a few thousand rupiah to cross their land, which is normal. The swings are separate businesses with their own prices.

The waterfalls of north Bali are bigger and quieter than the ones around Ubud, and further away: Sekumpul, Banyumala, Gitgit and the falls around Munduk are all roughly two hours from Ubud on the road over the mountains past the lakes. Sekumpul is the largest on the island at about 80 metres, and reaching the base means a steep descent of several hundred steps and a river crossing, so it is a walk rather than a viewpoint stop. Munduk sits at around 800 metres, which makes it noticeably cooler and often misty in the afternoon. Days up here usually pair a waterfall with the lake temple at Ulun Danu Beratan and the Handara Gate.

Pura Penataran Agung Lempuyang is the first of seven temples climbing Mount Lempuyang in Karangasem, east Bali, and its split gate frames Mount Agung on a clear morning. The famous mirror-image photograph is made by a photographer at the gate holding a piece of glass under a phone; there is no lake. That photograph is the reason for the queue, which runs to two hours or more from mid-morning, so tours leave Ubud around 5:00 to be there when it opens. A shuttle runs from the car park up to the temple, a sarong is required, and Agung is most often clear before nine. East Bali days usually continue to Tirta Gangga water palace and the Taman Ujung palace on the coast.

The jungle swings near Ubud are a cluster of businesses along the Ayung river gorge around Bongkasa and along the road above Tegallalang, each with several swings of different heights, from about 10 metres up to 78 metres at the tallest, plus nests, hanging beds and photo props. You are strapped into a harness and pushed by staff, and the swing arcs out over the gorge. Prices are per swing or as a package, flowing dresses are rented on site for photographs, and the queue on a busy afternoon is the real cost, so an early slot is the one to book.

The animal parks near Ubud are in Gianyar: Bali Zoo at Singapadu, Bali Safari and Marine Park on the coast road east, and the Mason Elephant Park at Taro, which keeps a herd of Sumatran elephants rescued from logging camps. Bali Bird Park at Batubulan holds around a thousand birds, including a large collection of Indonesian species and birds of paradise, in walk-through aviaries. Turtle conservation sits on the south coast at Serangan and Kuta. All are open daily, most from 9:00, and the safari park's tram circuits and animal shows run to a timetable, so check times if there is one you want.

A Balinese village day is about the compound and the rice cycle. A family compound is a walled group of pavilions around a household temple, laid out to a fixed pattern with the shrine to the mountain side; the kitchen and the rice barn have their own places in it. Around it the paddies run on the subak calendar, planting, flooding, harvesting and drying on the road, and the fields are worked by hand and by hand tractor. Mornings start early: the market at dawn, the offerings, breakfast of rice and coffee. Visits like this are hosted by the family, and a few words of Indonesian, a sarong for the temple and shoes off at the door are the courtesies that matter.

A highlights day around Ubud strings together the places that photograph best in the order the light suits them: Tegallalang before the coaches, a swing while the queue is short, a waterfall by late morning, and Tirta Empul or a temple in the afternoon. The distances are small but the roads are slow, so the order matters more than the list. Sarongs are needed at every temple and are provided at the gate; swings and some viewpoints charge separately from the tour; and wet-season afternoons, November to March, often bring rain from about two o'clock, which is why these days start early.

Ubud's reputation as Bali's art town dates from the 1930s, when the painters Walter Spies and Rudolf Bonnet settled here and, with the royal family, founded the Pita Maha artists' association that shaped the Ubud painting style. The Neka, Puri Lukisan and ARMA museums hold the best collections, and the villages around the town still specialise: Batuan in painting, Mas in carving, Celuk in silver. Studio workshops take that into a few hours of making something yourself with an instructor, and you leave with the piece. Wear something that can take paint, wax or dye.

Pura Luhur Uluwatu stands on a cliff about 70 metres above the sea at the south-western tip of the Bukit peninsula, one of Bali's six directional temples, associated with the eleventh-century priest Empu Kuturan. Tirta Empul is a water temple on the Pakerisan river at Tampaksiring, founded in 962 AD around a spring the Balinese hold sacred. The purification ritual, melukat, means entering the pool and moving from spout to spout under the water in order; two of the spouts are reserved for funeral rites and are not used, and a guide will show you which. Sarongs are provided at the entrance, and you will want a change of clothes for afterwards. The temple is busiest with local worshippers around full moon and on Balinese holy days, which is worth knowing rather than avoiding. The presidential palace built by Sukarno in the 1950s stands on the hill directly above the springs.

Ubud's reputation as Bali's art town dates from the 1930s, when the painters Walter Spies and Rudolf Bonnet settled here and, with the royal family, founded the Pita Maha artists' association that shaped the Ubud painting style. The Neka, Puri Lukisan and ARMA museums hold the best collections, and the villages around the town still specialise: Batuan in painting, Mas in carving, Celuk in silver. Studio workshops take that into a few hours of making something yourself with an instructor, and you leave with the piece. Wear something that can take paint, wax or dye.

The waterfalls around Ubud sit in a band to the east and south of the town, mostly within an hour's drive. Tegenungan is the closest and the busiest, with a broad fall and a pool at the bottom. Tibumana and Kanto Lampo, both in Bangli, are smaller and better for getting in the water: Tibumana drops in a single curtain into a clear pool, and at Kanto Lampo the water fans across a stepped rock face that people climb onto for photographs. All of them involve steps down and back up, and the rocks are slippery, so proper sandals or shoes that can get wet are the right footwear. The wet season, November to March, brings the fullest flow but also brown water for a day or two after heavy rain.

Tibumana and Kanto Lampo, both in Bangli, are smaller and better for getting in the water: Tibumana drops in a single curtain into a clear pool, and at Kanto Lampo the water fans across a stepped rock face that people climb onto for photographs. All of them involve steps down and back up, and the rocks are slippery, so proper sandals or shoes that can get wet are the right footwear. The wet season, November to March, brings the fullest flow but also brown water for a day or two after heavy rain.

Osaka is Japan's kitchen: the city that invented takoyaki, okonomiyaki and kushikatsu, and Dotonbori's canal of neon signs is where it eats them. Osaka is the base for day trips to Nara, Kobe, Himeji and Koyasan, all under an hour and a half. The city is louder and cheaper than Kyoto and its people are known for it.

Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Park sits on the ground beneath the point where the bomb detonated at 8:15 on 6 August 1945. The A-Bomb Dome, the skeleton of the industrial promotion hall, was left as it stood; the Peace Memorial Museum reopened in 2019 after a redesign and takes about two hours, and is not for young children. The Children's Peace Monument is hung with paper cranes sent from around the world. Hiroshima's own food is okonomiyaki layered with noodles, eaten at counters in Okonomimura. Miyajima is 40 minutes away and most visitors combine the two in one day.

Miyajima, properly Itsukushima, is the island in Hiroshima Bay whose shrine stands on stilts over the water with its great torii gate in the sea, rebuilt in 1875 and restored in 2022. The gate is walked to at low tide and floats at high tide, and the tide table decides what you see; both are worth it. Deer roam the village, the ropeway climbs Mount Misen for the view over the Inland Sea, and the local foods are grilled oysters and momiji manju maple cakes. From Hiroshima it is a tram or train to Miyajimaguchi and a ten-minute ferry, about 40 minutes in all, or a direct boat from the Peace Park.

Thailand's two great festivals fall at opposite ends of the year. Ayutthaya was the capital of Siam for 417 years until the Burmese sacked it in 1767, and its ruins, 80 kilometres north of Bangkok, are a UNESCO site of brick prangs and headless Buddhas spread across an island in the river. The Buddha head held in the roots of a bodhi tree at Wat Mahathat is the image everyone comes for, and the etiquette is to crouch so your head is lower than its own. Wat Chaiwatthanaram on the riverbank is the best-preserved complex and is lit at night. The heat is fierce by 11:00; tours that start early and use a bicycle or a tuk-tuk between temples see more than those on foot.

Da Nang is the central coast's city, a 30-kilometre beach from the Son Tra peninsula to the Marble Mountains, and it is where the day trips of central Vietnam start. Ba Na Hills, 40 kilometres west, is a French hill station rebuilt as a theme park at 1,400 metres, reached by one of the world's longest cable cars, with the Golden Bridge held up by two giant stone hands; go early, it is cool and crowded. The Marble Mountains are five limestone hills of caves and pagodas with a view over the coast. Son Tra has the 67-metre Lady Buddha and the last red-shanked douc langurs. The Hai Van Pass, the road north to Hue, is the most scenic drive in the country, done by motorbike or car with stops at the old French and American bunkers on the summit.

Ha Long Bay is some 1,600 limestone islands and pillars rising out of the Gulf of Tonkin, a UNESCO site since 1994, and the way to see it is from the water: day cruises out of Tuan Chau or Ha Long harbour run six to eight hours with a cave (Sung Sot or Thien Cung), a kayak or bamboo-boat paddle into a lagoon, and lunch on board; overnight cruises push further out and are the better experience, with the bay empty at dawn. Lan Ha Bay, south of Cat Ba island, has the same karst with a fraction of the boats and is where the newer cruises go. Bai Tu Long, to the north-east, is the quietest of the three. The bay is misty and cool from December to February and clearest from March to May and September to November; the 2.5-hour expressway from Hanoi has made day trips routine.

Lan Ha Bay, south of Cat Ba island, has the same karst with a fraction of the boats and is where the newer cruises go. Bai Tu Long, to the north-east, is the quietest of the three. The bay is misty and cool from December to February and clearest from March to May and September to November; the 2.5-hour expressway from Hanoi has made day trips routine.

Hanoi is a thousand years old and a French colonial capital and it is both at once: the Old Quarter's 36 streets each named for the guild that traded there, the lake of the returned sword at its heart, the Temple of Literature from 1070, the mausoleum where Ho Chi Minh lies in state (mornings only, closed Mondays and Fridays and for two months each autumn), and the tree-lined French quarter of villas and the Opera House. The Train Street cafes, where the railway runs a metre from the tables, open and close as the authorities change their minds. Egg coffee was invented here in 1946, bun cha is the lunch, and the water-puppet theatre by the lake is the evening. Hanoi is cool and grey from December to February and hot from May to September; October and November are the months.

Sa Pa sits at 1,600 metres in the Hoang Lien mountains near the Chinese border, a French hill station of the 1920s that is now the base for trekking through the terraced valleys of the Hmong, Dao and Giay villages. The classic walk drops from town through Cat Cat or Y Linh Ho to Lao Chai and Ta Van along the Muong Hoa valley, five to six hours, with lunch in a village house and an overnight in a homestay for the two-day version; local Hmong women guide most treks and the trails are muddy after rain. Fansipan, Indochina's highest peak at 3,143 metres, is a cable car of 15 minutes or a two-day climb. The terraces are flooded and mirror-like in May and June and gold in September; December to February is cold, often fogged, and occasionally snows. Bac Ha's Sunday market is the big Flower Hmong market, two hours away.

The classic walk drops from town through Cat Cat or Y Linh Ho to Lao Chai and Ta Van along the Muong Hoa valley, five to six hours, with lunch in a village house and an overnight in a homestay for the two-day version; local Hmong women guide most treks and the trails are muddy after rain. Fansipan, Indochina's highest peak at 3,143 metres, is a cable car of 15 minutes or a two-day climb. The terraces are flooded and mirror-like in May and June and gold in September; December to February is cold, often fogged, and occasionally snows. Bac Ha's Sunday market is the big Flower Hmong market, two hours away.

The Cu Chi tunnels, 60 kilometres north-west of Ho Chi Minh City, are a 250-kilometre network dug by the Viet Cong from the 1940s and used through the American war as living quarters, hospitals, kitchens and a route into Saigon itself; the district was carpet-bombed and defoliated without ever being cleared. Two sites are open, Ben Dinh (closer, busier) and Ben Duoc (the original, quieter, with a memorial temple); both show the trapdoors, the booby traps, a widened section of tunnel visitors can crawl through for 20 to 100 metres, and a shooting range where the AK-47 fire is audible across the whole site. Half-day tours run morning and afternoon, often by speedboat up the Saigon River, and are usually combined with the Mekong or the city.

The Mekong Delta begins two hours south of Ho Chi Minh City, where the river splits into nine channels across a flat green province of rice, coconut and fruit orchards. Day tours reach My Tho and Ben Tre: a boat on the main river, a sampan through the coconut-palm creeks, a coconut-candy workshop, honey tea and fruit with folk music, and a bicycle or tuk-tuk through the orchards. The floating markets are further: Cai Be has faded to a handful of boats, while Cai Rang at Can Tho, four hours from the city, is the real one and only works from 5:00 to 8:00, so it needs an overnight in Can Tho. The delta is hot and humid all year; the wet season, May to November, is when the orchards are fullest.

The Cu Chi tunnels, 60 kilometres north-west of Ho Chi Minh City, are a 250-kilometre network dug by the Viet Cong from the 1940s and used through the American war as living quarters, hospitals, kitchens and a route into Saigon itself; the district was carpet-bombed and defoliated without ever being cleared. Two sites are open, Ben Dinh (closer, busier) and Ben Duoc (the original, quieter, with a memorial temple); both show the trapdoors, the booby traps, a widened section of tunnel visitors can crawl through for 20 to 100 metres, and a shooting range where the AK-47 fire is audible across the whole site. Half-day tours run morning and afternoon, often by speedboat up the Saigon River, and are usually combined with the Mekong or the city.

The price covers Free Hotel pickup and drop-off in district 1, 3, 4, 5, Air-conditioned transportation, tour guide, Documentary viewing at Cu Chi and Tapioca and tea tasting. The Mekong Delta begins two hours south of Ho Chi Minh City, where the river splits into nine channels across a flat green province of rice, coconut and fruit orchards. Day tours reach My Tho and Ben Tre: a boat on the main river, a sampan through the coconut-palm creeks, a coconut-candy workshop, honey tea and fruit with folk music, and a bicycle or tuk-tuk through the orchards. The floating markets are further: Cai Be has faded to a handful of boats, while Cai Rang at Can Tho, four hours from the city, is the real one and only works from 5:00 to 8:00, so it needs an overnight in Can Tho. The delta is hot and humid all year; the wet season, May to November, is when the orchards are fullest.
